course.oneline: The five layers of gen AI and Google Cloud's options at each, and how to choose and maintain solutions; exam questions test layer roles and which tool fits which need.

key.d: Top to bottom: **Gen AI powered applications** are the user-facing frontend. **Agents** take autonomous action. The **platform** is the glue. **Models** are the brain. **Infrastructure** is the foundation (servers, GPUs, TPUs).

A **gen AI agent** is an application that tries to achieve a goal by observing the world and acting upon it with **tools**. **Reasoning loop**: Observe, Interpret, Plan, Act, repeated until goal or stopping point.

**Conversational agents** hold dialogue with users, inferring **intent** and calling tools if needed. **Workflow agents** automate multi-step tasks: you define a task or trigger a process, and they execute actions via **APIs**.

**Agent Platform** (exam: Vertex AI) is the unified ML platform to build, deploy and manage ML and gen AI. MLOps tools: **Feature Store**, **Model Registry**, Model Evaluation, Agent Platform Pipelines, **Model Monitoring**.

key.t: Model Garden or build your own
key.d: Most organisations don't need a new model: **Model Garden** lets you discover, customise and deploy Google, third-party and open-source models. To build: **custom training** (any framework) or **AutoML** (minimal technical knowledge).

Hardware and software to train, deploy and scale models: **GPUs** and **TPUs** (Google's custom AI chips) for parallel processing, **hypercomputers**, high-performance storage, and Google's high-bandwidth, low-latency global fiber network.

**Edge computing** runs AI close to the data source: real-time responsiveness, increased data privacy, less reliance on internet connectivity. Tools: **LiteRT** (on-device runtime) and **Gemini Nano**; Agent Platform still builds, trains and deploys.

Assess **scale**, **customisation**, user interaction, privacy and resources (**time, people, budget**). Costs: training, deploying, using the model. Pre-built apps take seconds; fully custom solutions take months; plan maintenance from the start.

watch: Course says agents 'independently set goals'; in practice an agent pursues a given goal, deciding its own steps and tools.
Model vs agent: generating or understanding content is a model; multi-step orchestration, personalisation over time and actions are an agent.
Specialised domains: fresh or proprietary **facts** → RAG/**grounding**; domain style, format or behaviour → **fine-tuning**.
Exam guide's AI-optimised infrastructure: **hypercomputer**, Google's custom-designed **TPUs**, **GPUs**, data centres, cloud computing.

3.1.gist: Introduction to Course 3: why decision-makers need a high-level view of the gen AI landscape, and the questions the course answers.
points: User-facing apps only **scratch the surface** of gen AI; you can **build a custom solution** or use **pre-existing tools** such as Google Cloud's.
Whether or not they are developers, decision-makers must understand **what's possible** to decide well.
Three questions: the **layers** of gen AI solutions, the **Google Cloud options** available, and when to choose one solution over another.
Covers the **gen AI landscape** at a high level, not technical detail; Courses 1 and 2 are recommended first.

3.2.gist: Presents the five layers gen AI is built on, from user-facing applications down to infrastructure, and the role of each.
points: **Gen AI powered applications** are the user-facing **frontend**; **agents** take autonomous action, handling multi-step tasks a model alone can't.
An **agent** is software that learns how best to achieve a goal from its inputs and the tools available, deciding without constant human input.
The **platform** is the backbone or glue between agents and models, providing APIs, data management and model deployment tools while hiding infrastructure complexity.
**Models** are the agent's brain, trained on vast data; **infrastructure** is the foundation: servers, GPUs, TPUs and software to store and run models.

3.3.gist: Defines gen AI agents, what they add to applications, and how agents and applications split roles, including multi-agent systems.
points: A **gen AI agent** is an application that tries to achieve a goal by observing the world and acting upon it using its **tools**.
Agents bring three things: **understanding and responding to natural language**, **automating complex tasks**, and **personalisation**.
Agents add intelligence and automation; **applications** provide the framework and purpose (UI, goals, tasks). A **multi-agent system** combines specialised agents in one app.
Use **pre-built** or **custom** agents; **AI Applications** (Google Cloud) creates agents with natural language instead of complex code.

3.4.gist: Explains the two categories of agents, conversational and workflow, their five-step flows, and six agent use-case families.
points: **Conversational agents** understand what you mean, not just what you say: input → understand **intent** → call a tool if needed → generate → deliver.
**Workflow agents** automate tasks or complex processes: a task or trigger → interpret requirements → execute actions (often via **APIs**) → generate result → deliver it.
Six use-case families: customer service, employee productivity, creative, code, data and **security agents** (which can create **detection rules**).
Key distinction: **conversational** = dialogue with users; **workflow** = automating multi-step tasks. Automated research example: **Gemini Deep Research**.

3.5.gist: Shows what makes an agent more than a model: a reasoning loop plus tools, enabling multi-step work beyond text generation.
points: Agents = **model + reasoning loop + tools**; they solve complex problems with **minimal human intervention** and manage multi-step tasks LLMs alone can't.
The **reasoning loop** (Observe, Interpret, Plan, Act) repeats until the goal or a stopping point; frameworks include **ReAct** and **chain-of-thought (CoT)**.
**Tools** are functions letting the agent interact with its environment: update inventory, schedule meetings, auto-order supplies, talk to a robot's sensors and actuators.
Rule of thumb: generating or understanding content = **model**; multi-step orchestration, personalisation over time or actions = **agent**.

3.6.gist: Covers the platform layer, the 'glue' of gen AI, through Agent Platform (exam: Vertex AI) and its MLOps tools.
points: **Agent Platform** provides infrastructure, pre-trained models and tools to build, deploy and manage ML and gen AI, bringing pieces together easily and scalably.
Six features: open and flexible (**no vendor lock-in**), powerful infrastructure, pre-trained models, comprehensive tooling, customisation via **built-in IDE**, easy integration via **APIs**.
**MLOps** automates, standardises and manages the ML project lifecycle; Agent Platform adds fully managed compute, distributed training, hyperparameter optimisation and enterprise security.

**Feature Store** shares features; **Model Registry** manages versions; Model Evaluation compares models; Agent Platform Pipelines automate ML workflows; **Model Monitoring** detects degradation, skew and drift.

3.7.gist: Covers the model layer: using existing models from Model Garden versus building your own with custom training or AutoML on Agent Platform.
points: Most organisations don't need a new model: **Model Garden** lets you discover, customise and deploy Google, third-party and open-source models.

First-party **foundation models**: Gemini, **Imagen** (text-to-image), **Veo** (text-to-video, image-to-video), Chirp 2.0 (speech-to-text); also pre-trained APIs, open models (Gemma 2) and third-party (Claude).
Build your own: **fully custom training** with any ML framework (PyTorch, TensorFlow…), or **AutoML** for image, video and tabular data with minimal technical knowledge.
Decision rule: ready, high-performing option on a moderate budget → **Model Garden**; full control of architecture and training → custom model on Agent Platform.

3.8.gist: Fictitious Cymbal Aerospace case: using Agent Platform AutoML and Gemini to extract and explain metadata from 3D CAD models of jet engine components.
points: Problem: extracting material composition, dimensions, stress points and tolerances from **3D CAD models** was manual, slow and error-prone.
Layer 1: **Agent Platform AutoML** trains a specialised model to extract key metadata from CAD files, with no deep ML expertise needed.
Layer 2: **Gemini** within Agent Platform, integrated via MLOps tools such as **Agent Platform Pipelines**, turns raw metadata into natural-language summaries and answers.
Platform benefits: simplified model development, customised solutions on own data, efficient scaling, streamlined **serverless** deployment with Agent Platform handling MLOps.

3.9.gist: Covers the infrastructure layer: the hardware and software for compute, storage and networking needed to train, deploy and scale AI models.
points: **GPUs** (originally graphics rendering) and **TPUs** (Google's custom AI-optimised chips) excel at **parallel processing**, crucial for training large neural networks.
A **hypercomputer** links many GPU/TPU nodes over high-speed networks into one massive supercomputer for the most demanding gen AI models.
Gen AI is **data hungry**: storage needs high throughput, scalability, reliability and durability, and fast access; Google's **global fiber network** gives high-bandwidth, low-latency links.
Without a platform handling it, infrastructure matters at every stage (data collection, training, refinement, deployment, monitoring); benefits: **scalability, performance, cost-effectiveness**.

3.10.gist: Covers edge computing: running AI on devices close to the data source, Google's edge tools, and when to choose edge over cloud.
points: **Edge computing** runs AI closer to the data source or point of need: **real-time responsiveness**, increased data privacy, less reliance on internet connectivity.
**Gemini Nano**, Google's most efficient, compact model, runs on-device (privacy, speed, offline access), e.g. Pixel Call Notes; Android developers use the **AI Edge SDK**.
**Agent Platform** builds and refines models, then converts them to **LiteRT** (on-device runtime), packages them in containers, and manages and monitors edge deployments.
Edge for instant, on-device decisions (surgical device, self-driving car); cloud for scale or centralised analysis (high-volume chatbot, smart-city traffic).

3.11.gist: Covers how to decide between existing and custom gen AI solutions by assessing needs and resources: people, cost and time.
points: Assess **scale**, **customisation** (grounding or fine-tuning, or a new model?), interaction (latency, connectivity) and resources: time, people, budget.

**Business leaders** use pre-built solutions (Google Workspace with Gemini); **developers** build custom agents (AI Applications, pre-trained APIs, Agent Platform); **AI practitioners** customise and optimise models.
You pay for **training**, deploying and using models; pricing: **usage-based** (tokens or characters), subscription-based, licensing fees, free tiers.
Time: pre-built app, **seconds**; custom agent with AI Applications, much less than fully custom; fully custom solution with custom model, **months**.

3.12.gist: Lists the needs to assess before starting a gen AI solution: scale, customisation, user interaction, privacy, plus latency, connectivity, accuracy and explainability.
points: **Scale**: small teams go far with **pre-built tools**; millions of customers need a robust, customised solution with scalability and security.
**Customisation**: start with existing models and **fine-tune**; for specialised domains, fresh or proprietary facts → **RAG/grounding**, domain style or behaviour → fine-tuning.
Also assess **privacy** (encryption, access controls, GDPR, HIPAA), **latency**, connectivity (offline → edge), accuracy and **explainability** (healthcare, finance).
Short on time, some coding skills, need text-to-image for a campaign → **pre-trained API**; fine-tuning costs time, building from scratch is wrong.

3.13.gist: Covers how to compare gen AI providers and models, and why maintenance must be planned from the start.
points: Compare providers in four steps: evaluate capabilities with **benchmarks**, compare **pricing structures**, factor in additional costs (storage, API calls, fine-tuning), read the fine print.
Where to compare: provider pricing pages, research papers and independent benchmarks, community forums and discussions.
Maintenance is "a journey, not a destination": plan it from the start; **Google Cloud's fully managed environment** lets developers focus on agent development.
Maintenance areas: **model monitoring and retraining**, data updates, software updates and bug fixes, hardware and infrastructure (**capacity planning**), security and compliance.
